title: The DSM-5-TR: Overview
description: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR, published 2022 by the American Psychiatric Association) is the standard classification of mental disorders used by US clinicians. It organizes disorders into chapters (neurodevelopmental, psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, OCD-related, trauma, dissociative, somatic, feeding/eating, sleep-wake, substance, personality, and others), each with documented diagnostic criteria. The DSM is a clinical consensus document — revised as evidence evolves — and its categories are tools for communication among professionals, not verdicts on persons.
classification: DSM-5-TR (2022), American Psychiatric Association — classification system, not a single disorder.
symptoms: Not applicable — the DSM defines criteria sets per disorder; this record describes the system itself.
history_notes: Evolved from DSM-I (1952) through DSM-II, III (1980 — criteria-based turn), III-R, IV, IV-TR, 5 (2013), to 5-TR (2022). Each revision reflects advancing evidence and ongoing debate.
treatments: Not applicable to the system itself; treatment information appears per-disorder in the companion databases.

title: The ICD-11: Overview
description: The International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11, World Health Organization, effective 2022) is the global standard for health statistics, including mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders (Chapter 06). Used worldwide for reporting and in many countries for clinical coding, it parallels the DSM while differing in some categories and criteria — the two systems are harmonized where evidence allows. The ICD’s mental-health chapter reflects global consensus, including cultural considerations in how disorders present across societies.
classification: ICD-11 Chapter 06 (2022), World Health Organization — global classification system.
symptoms: Not applicable — system-level record; criteria live per-disorder.
history_notes: ICD lineage reaches back to the 19th century; mental disorders entered in ICD-6 (1949); ICD-10 (1990s) to ICD-11 (2022) brought dimensional elements and global field testing.
treatments: System-level record; per-disorder treatment information in companion databases.

title: A Brief History of Classification
description: Documented history: before modern classifications, mental suffering was described through moral, spiritual, and early medical lenses. The 19th century brought asylum medicine and early nosologies (Kraepelin’s dementia praecox/manic-depressive distinction, ~1899). The 20th century saw psychoanalytic formulations, then the DSM-III’s 1980 criteria-based revolution — explicit symptom lists enabling reliable diagnosis and research. The 21st century adds neuroscience, genetics, and dimensional models (e.g., HiTOP, RDoC as research frameworks) — classification remains an active science.
classification: Historical record — the development of psychiatric classification.
history_notes: Key documented milestones: Kraepelin (1899), DSM-I (1952), DSM-III (1980), ICD-10 (1992), DSM-5 (2013), ICD-11/DSM-5-TR (2022); research frameworks RDoC (NIMH) and HiTOP ongoing.
treatments: Historical record; modern treatment information per-disorder in companion databases.

title: Epidemiology: How Common Are These Conditions?
t: Epidemiology: How Common Are These Conditions?
description: Documented public-health data: the WHO reports that roughly 1 in 8 people globally live with a mental disorder; anxiety and depression are the most common. National surveys (e.g., US NSDUH, WHO World Mental Health surveys) track prevalence by disorder, age, and region. These figures describe populations — they say nothing about any individual — and they undercount where stigma suppresses reporting. Epidemiology guides policy and services, never diagnosis.
classification: Population-health record — prevalence statistics, not a disorder.
history_notes: Modern psychiatric epidemiology began with mid-20th-century community surveys (e.g., Stirling County, ECA in the 1980s) and continues via WHO and national surveillance.

title: How Diagnoses Are Made (Documented Process)
description: Documented clinical process: qualified professionals diagnose through clinical interviews, documented criteria comparison, history-taking, and — where indicated — ruling out medical causes; structured instruments may support but never replace clinical judgment. Diagnosis is a professional act within a therapeutic relationship, not a checklist exercise — and the DSM itself cautions against cookbook application. This record describes the process generally; it does not enable self-diagnosis, which the framework forbids.
